summary.text: The received pictographic account relates 了 to 子, describing it as 子 without arms; later commentary reads it as crossed or entangled legs. The character also writes “finish,” but how that word became associated with the graph remains disputed.

formation.text: The received analysis treats 了 as a pictograph related to 子, with the arms omitted. Later commentary interprets the form as crossed or entangled legs. These are competing interpretations, not confirmed depictions of an early inscription.

history.text: The received account describes the graph in relation to 子; later commentary offers a crossed- or entangled-legs reading. The cited accounts do not establish a securely dated earliest form or a sequence of graphic changes.

uncertainties.text: The word “finish” may have been written with 了 because it sounded like the old name of the depicted form, but neither that name nor the sound match is verified. A proposed route from entanglement through tying to completion also lacks dated intermediate examples.

Accounts trace the completed-action particle to Tang–Song usage, but the cited summaries do not provide dated primary examples. A possible interaction between sentence-final 了 and 也 in some dialects remains tentative.

senses.text: The received entry glosses 了 with 尦; later commentary interprets this as legs crossing or becoming entangled. This is a historical interpretation, not direct confirmation of what an early inscription depicted.

Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed”; a Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the pictographic interpretations remain unresolved.
